input_signals.name: EVCashYieldMinusWCBuildup
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che)), NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(wcap, che), 1), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A low enterprise multiple is attractive only if the operating profit behind it is not being generated by inflating non-cash working capital; balance-sheet accrual buildup signals that EBITDA overstates distributable cash.
input_signals.reasoning: Using EV (equity plus debt minus cash) makes the valuation leg capital-structure neutral and directly comparable to EBITDA, while the change in non-cash working capital (wcap net of cash) is the balance-sheet measure of accruals that pollutes EBITDA. Combining a high EBITDA/EV rank with a low working-capital-accrual rank targets firms that are cheap on cash-generating operations rather than on accounting-inflated operating income.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( ebitda, sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), che ) ), neg( ratio( delta( sub( wcap, che ), 1 ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: SalesYieldNonCashCurrentAssetDrag
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), sale)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A low price-to-sales multiple is a bargain only when revenue is collected rather than parked in receivables and inventory; firms whose non-cash current assets balloon relative to sales are recognizing revenue that has not converted to cash.
input_signals.reasoning: The revenue-quality leg is now built from balance-sheet items with broad coverage (act, che, sale) instead of the sparse and sign-inconsistent cash-flow-statement components, and it excludes payables entirely so that stretching suppliers can no longer masquerade as high quality. Scaling the change in non-cash current assets by sales makes the two legs conceptually matched: both are per-dollar-of-revenue measures, so the composite isolates cheap firms whose revenue base is genuinely cash-converting.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( sale, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), neg( ratio( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), sale ) ) )

input_signals.name: ValueConditionedBalanceSheetAccrual
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Accounting quality is priced least efficiently inside the value tail; among cheap firms, low balance-sheet accruals identify genuine bargains and high accruals identify value traps, while among glamour firms the accrual signal carries little incremental information.
input_signals.reasoning: The bounded cheapness rank acts as a conditioning weight (near zero for expensive and negative-book-equity firms, so no sign pathology), and the signed, winsorized balance-sheet accrual z-score supplies direction, so the long-short spread is long cheap-and-clean versus short cheap-and-dirty. Because both legs sit in the value/low-price region, HML and CMA loadings largely cancel, which is exactly the structural fix for the near-zero FF5 alphas of generation 0's additive composites.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), zscore( winsor( neg( ratio( sub( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( sub( lct, dlc ), txp ), 1 ) ), dp ), at ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: ValueWithStableWorkingCapital
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(VOL(RATIO(wcap, at), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Erratic working capital signals opaque, hard-to-audit accounting, so investors rationally discount such firms; cheap firms with smooth working-capital intensity are more likely to be genuine mispricings whose value discount closes.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs the invalidated second-moment idea using an accrual-exclusive state variable (wcap) whose five-year volatility is computable from annual balance sheets with wide coverage. It tests an information-risk mechanism rather than an accrual-level mechanism, so if the level-based composites keep getting absorbed by FF5, a dispersion-based accounting-opacity leg tells us something new about which cheap firms are traps.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), neg( vol( ratio( wcap, at ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: ValueWithNOWCAtOwnHistoryLow
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), at), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Working-capital norms differ enormously across business models, so what matters is whether a firm's non-cash working capital sits high or low relative to its own five-year history; cheap firms whose balance sheet is currently lean by their own standard have already worked off past accruals and face no reversal drag.
input_signals.reasoning: This drops the discredited "linear-in-B/M" construction and replaces the cross-sectional accrual level with a within-firm time-series position (TS_RANK), which removes industry and business-model differences in normal working-capital intensity that contaminate cross-sectional accrual ranks. It is therefore mechanistically distinct from the archive's cross-sectional level, flow, and volatility legs, and it avoids negative-numerator distress artifacts because the valuation leg keeps standard book equity.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), neg( ts_rank( ratio( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), at ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: DepreciationConservatismValue
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ni, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(dp, at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Depreciation is the largest non-discretionary negative accrual; firms that depreciate aggressively relative to industry peers understate reported earnings, so a high earnings yield achieved despite conservative accounting understates true cash profitability and is systematically underpriced.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the mirror image of the usual accrual story and is not a reconstruction of cash-flow-to-price: the signal deliberately rewards a *large* negative accrual, so it separates firms that are cheap because earnings are conservatively stated from firms that are cheap on inflated income. Industry z-scoring of dp/at is essential because depreciation intensity mostly reflects capital intensity, and it makes the accounting-conservatism component orthogonal to sector composition.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( ni, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), ind_zscore( ratio( dp, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: EarningsYieldAsymmetricAccrualPenalty
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ni, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(MUL(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at), INDICATOR(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), 0))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Only income-increasing accruals carry manipulation content; working-capital releases (negative accruals) reflect operating discipline or conservatism rather than inflated earnings, so the value signal should be penalized for accrual build-ups but not symmetrically rewarded for run-downs.
input_signals.reasoning: The tax-payable leg is abandoned because, as noted, Δtxp is itself a current-liability accrual and too small and sparse to carry half the signal weight; it is replaced by a positive-part accrual penalty built with INDICATOR, which imposes an economically motivated asymmetry rather than a linear accrual rank. This isolates a specific design question the archive cannot answer: whether the value-trap effect is driven entirely by the income-increasing tail of accruals.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( ni, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), neg( mul( ratio( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), at ), indicator( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), 0 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: SalesYieldReceivableGrowthDivergence
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(SUB(GROWTH(SUB(act, che), 1), GROWTH(sale, 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Revenue quality is revealed by whether non-cash current assets grow faster than the revenue they support; a low price-to-sales multiple is a genuine bargain only when receivables and inventory are not outrunning sales.
input_signals.reasoning: This fixes the cash-contamination flaw by explicitly excluding che from the working-capital measure, so cash accumulation no longer looks like accrual bloat, and it changes the statistic rather than the horizon: a growth-rate divergence is scale-free and directly matched to the sales-based valuation leg, unlike an asset-scaled level change. The receivables-versus-sales growth gap is the classic revenue-recognition red flag, giving a clean test of whether cheap-on-sales firms with deteriorating revenue quality are the traps.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( sale, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), neg( sub( growth( sub( act, che ), 1 ), growth( sale, 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ValuePremiumGatedByCleanAccruals
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The value premium exists only where reported fundamentals are trustworthy: among clean-accrual firms cheapness predicts high returns, while among accrual-inflated firms book value is unreliable and the value spread should be flat or perverse.
input_signals.reasoning: This inverts the conditioning of the archive's only alpha-positive signal — accrual quality becomes the bounded gate and signed cheapness carries direction — so the long-short spread is long cheap-clean versus short expensive-clean, holding accounting quality high in both legs. Comparing its alpha to ValueConditionedBalanceSheetAccrual identifies whether the interaction is a value effect concentrated in clean firms or an accrual effect concentrated in cheap firms, which is the single most informative unresolved design question in the archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( ratio( sub( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( sub( lct, dlc ), txp ), 1 ) ), dp ), at ) ) ), zscore( winsor( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: ValueWithGrossOperatingBalanceSheetChurn
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(ADD(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), sale), RATIO(DELTA(SUB(lct, dlc), 1), sale))), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Sloan accruals net asset-side buildup against liability-side buildup, but for a cheap firm both are bad news: growing receivables and inventory signal unsold or uncollected revenue, while growing payables and accrued liabilities signal stretched suppliers and funding strain, so the two should enter with the same sign rather than opposite signs.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a decomposition test of the accrual leg itself: if the netted Sloan measure works only because of its asset side, then a gross-churn version that also penalizes operating-liability expansion should perform at least as well among value stocks and better in the distress tail. Sales scaling keeps both components commensurate with operating volume and avoids the capital-intensity contamination of asset scaling.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), zscore( winsor( neg( add( ratio( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), sale ), ratio( delta( sub( lct, dlc ), 1 ), sale ) ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: AssetSideAccrualGatedValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), at)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The value-trap effect comes from the asset side of accruals — receivables and inventory that represent revenue not yet collected or sold — while operating-liability growth is a financing/liquidity phenomenon that carries the opposite return sign.
input_signals.reasoning: The gross-churn test showed that adding operating-liability growth with a penalizing sign flips the FF5 alpha from +2.5% to −2.3%, which implies the liability side works in the opposite direction; the clean follow-up is to strip the liability side out entirely and see whether asset-side buildup alone reproduces or beats the netted Sloan measure. If it does, the mechanism is specifically about uncollected revenue and unsold inventory rather than total accrual accounting.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), zscore( winsor( neg( ratio( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), at ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: ChronicAccrualRelianceGatedValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(MA(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), 3)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A single year of accruals is a noisy read on accounting quality; what makes a cheap firm a trap is chronic, multi-year reliance on accruals to report income, and the average accrual rate over three years measures that reliance while preserving magnitude.
input_signals.reasoning: The persistence-count repair failed (alpha −1.9%) precisely because a 0–5 count throws away how large the accruals were, so the better fix is a magnitude-preserving three-year mean, which also reduces annual re-ranking and should raise the poor Sharpe (0.20) of the gated family. If chronic accrual reliance beats the one-year measure, the mechanism is a persistent reporting-policy effect rather than a one-year reversal effect.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), zscore( winsor( neg( ma( ratio( sub( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( sub( lct, dlc ), txp ), 1 ) ), dp ), at ), 3 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: EVYieldGatedAccrualQuality
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Accrual quality should be evaluated conditional on how cheap the firm's operating cash-generating capacity is relative to its whole capital structure, not on book-to-market, because the enterprise multiple identifies cheapness without the leverage and write-off distortions embedded in book equity.
input_signals.reasoning: Every gated signal so far has used a price-to-book or price-to-earnings gate, which is nearly collinear with HML, so the resulting spread earns alpha mainly through negative factor loadings while its raw return stays near zero (Sharpe 0.03–0.19); the EBITDA/EV gate was the archive's best raw-return valuation leg (Sharpe 0.283). Swapping the gate isolates whether the gated family's weak Sharpe is a HML-collinearity problem rather than an accrual-measurement problem.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ebitda, sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), che ) ) ), zscore( winsor( neg( ratio( sub( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( sub( lct, dlc ), txp ), 1 ) ), dp ), at ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: AccrualReversalCompletionGatedValue
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(MUL(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at)), INDICATOR(LAG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at), 1), 0)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: For a cheap firm the decisive question is where it stands in the accrual cycle: a firm that built up working capital last year and is now converting it into cash has already taken its earnings hit and is at the trough, whereas a firm that keeps accumulating after a prior build-up is on an escalating path of unsold inventory and uncollected receivables and its cheapness is a warning.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the cash-holdings idea with two-period accrual dynamics adds genuinely new content: the INDICATOR restricts attention to firms with a prior-year build-up, so the signed leg measures whether that specific excess is reversing or compounding, a stage-of-cycle concept absent from every archive entry (all of which use a level, average, count, volatility, or single change). Firms with no prior build-up receive zero and stay neutral, which sharpens the long and short legs onto the population where accrual reversal actually has predictive content.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), zscore( winsor( mul( neg( ratio( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), at ) ), indicator( lag( ratio( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), at ), 1 ), 0 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: EVYieldGatedReversalCompletion
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(MUL(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at)), INDICATOR(LAG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at), 1), 0)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What separates a cheap firm at the earnings trough from one still deteriorating is the stage of its accrual cycle: after a prior working-capital build-up, current release means the reversal has been taken and cash is arriving, while continued accumulation means the problem is compounding.
input_signals.reasoning: Reversal-completion was the accrual leg with the strongest cross-sectional slope in the archive (FMB 2.75) while the enterprise gate was the valuation leg with the best portfolio behaviour, so this pairing directly targets the FMB-versus-alpha tension that has characterized every generation. Because the indicator restricts the signed content to firms with a prior build-up, the sort concentrates where accrual reversal has genuine predictive content instead of ranking noise.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ebitda, sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), che ) ) ), zscore( winsor( mul( neg( ratio( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), at ) ), indicator( lag( ratio( delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ), at ), 1 ), 0 ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: DividendYieldGatedAccrualQuality
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dvc, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Dividend yield is the one valuation multiple whose numerator is cash that has already left the firm, so it cannot be inflated by accruals; among high-yield firms, accrual quality separates payouts funded by real cash generation from payouts being sustained while receivables and inventory swell.
input_signals.reasoning: All gates tested so far use accrual-contaminated numerators (book equity, reported earnings, EBITDA), which makes the gate itself partly endogenous to the accounting quality being measured; a cash-distribution gate breaks that circularity and is also less collinear with HML than book-to-market. The sustainability-of-payout mechanism is economically distinct from anything in the archive and coverage should be good since dvc is reported as zero rather than missing for non-payers.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( dvc, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), zscore( winsor( neg( ratio( sub( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( sub( lct, dlc ), txp ), 1 ) ), dp ), at ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: SalesToEnterpriseGatedAccrualQuality
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that are cheap relative to the revenue their capital supports are typically firms with temporarily depressed margins, and it is exactly in that population that accrual quality decides the outcome: a depressed-margin firm converting revenue into cash is a recovery candidate, while one whose thin profits rest on swelling receivables and inventory is a decaying business.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than tweaking the denominator of the archive's EBITDA/EV gate, this changes the gate's economic content from "cheap profit" to "cheap revenue," which selects a different and more margin-distressed population where the accrual mechanism should bite hardest, while keeping the capital-structure-neutral scaling that gave the enterprise gate its healthy raw spread. Revenue is also the least accounting-discretionary numerator available, so the gate is close to orthogonal to the accrual leg being tested, reducing the endogeneity that afflicts book-equity and earnings gates.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sale, sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), che ) ) ), zscore( winsor( neg( ratio( sub( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( sub( lct, dlc ), txp ), 1 ) ), dp ), at ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: LeveredIncomeIncreasingAccrualTrap
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(MUL(MUL(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), 0)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at)))), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Leverage does not make good accounting better, it makes bad accounting dangerous: only income-increasing accruals create a future reversal that must be absorbed while debt service continues, so among cheap firms the penalty for accrual-dependent earnings should scale with debt intensity and be switched off entirely for firms reporting conservative, income-decreasing accruals.
input_signals.reasoning: The asymmetry the critic identified is now explicit in the expression: INDICATOR keeps only the positive part of accruals, so firms with income-decreasing accruals receive a penalty of exactly zero regardless of leverage and no highly levered firm can be pushed into the long leg by its debt alone, which also removes the leverage main effect from the long side. Using the cross-sectional rank of debt intensity rather than its raw level prevents a handful of extremely levered firms from dominating the standardized leg while preserving the ordering that the amplification hypothesis requires.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ebitda, sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), che ) ) ), zscore( winsor( neg( mul( mul( ratio( sub( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( sub( lct, dlc ), txp ), 1 ) ), dp ), at ), indicator( ratio( sub( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( sub( lct, dlc ), txp ), 1 ) ), dp ), at ), 0 ) ), rank( ratio( add( dltt, dlc ), at ) ) ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: RevenueGatedIncomeIncreasingAccrualOnly
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(MUL(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), 0))), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Only income-increasing accruals create an obligation to reverse; income-decreasing accruals are conservatism and should earn no reward, so among firms cheap on revenue the short leg should be built purely from those inflating current earnings while the long leg holds all firms with no accrual inflation.
input_signals.reasoning: The levered asymmetric penalty produced the strongest cross-sectional slope in the entire archive (FMB 3.37) but a negative alpha, which localizes the problem in the leverage multiplier's low-leverage factor tilt rather than in the asymmetry; removing leverage and keeping the positive-part restriction should retain the slope while restoring the enterprise gate's alpha. It also directly tests whether the accrual side of the value-trap story is one-sided, a question the symmetric legs cannot answer.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sale, sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), che ) ) ), zscore( winsor( neg( mul( ratio( sub( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( sub( lct, dlc ), txp ), 1 ) ), dp ), at ), indicator( ratio( sub( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( sub( lct, dlc ), txp ), 1 ) ), dp ), at ), 0 ) ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: WorkingCapitalChargedEnterpriseYield
input_signals.expression: RATIO(SUB(ebitda, DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))
input_signals.hypothesis: The correct enterprise multiple charges operating profit for the working capital the business had to absorb to produce it, so a firm is cheap only if the profit remaining after that charge is large relative to total enterprise value.
input_signals.reasoning: Every enterprise-gated signal in the archive uses a [0,1] rank gate that flattens most of the cross-section and has repeatedly produced FMB t-stats of 0.3–2.6, whereas the archive's continuous-scale signals reliably delivered FMB t-stats above 3 but only ever used equity-market deflators, which are HML-collinear. This construction is continuous *and* enterprise-scaled, embedding the accrual correction in the numerator, so it is the natural test of whether the FMB weakness of the winning family is caused by the gate's functional form rather than its economics.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( sub( ebitda, delta( sub( sub( act, che ), sub( lct, dlc ) ), 1 ) ), sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), add( dltt, dlc ) ), che ) )

input_signals.name: RevenueGatedCollectionEfficiencyDecay
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(TREND(RATIO(SUB(act, che), sale), 5)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A single year's accrual build-up is mostly cyclical noise, but a multi-year upward drift in receivables-and-inventory per dollar of revenue is evidence of structural decay — lengthening collection periods and slower inventory turns — and a firm cheap on revenue with decaying collection efficiency is a business in decline rather than a mispriced asset.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has tested accrual levels, one-year changes, three-year means, five-year volatility, five-year own-history rank and distance-from-peak, but never a fitted multi-year *slope*, which is the only statistic that distinguishes persistent directional deterioration from mean-reverting fluctuation. The economic claim is new and specific to the revenue-multiple gate: cheapness on revenue is only a bargain if that revenue is still being converted to cash at a stable or improving rate.
input_signals.author: proposer

input_signals.name: RevenueGatedAccrualWithoutCashBuffer

input_signals.hypothesis: An accrual reversal is an accounting event for a cash-rich firm but a financing event for a cash-poor one, because the unwind of receivables and inventory has to be funded; the value trap is therefore the joint state of cheap price, income-increasing accruals, and no liquidity buffer to absorb the reversal.
input_signals.reasoning: This adds a genuinely new conditioning dimension — the balance-sheet liquidity cushion — rather than another deflator, and it is deliberately built to avoid the failure of the earlier leverage-weighted version: the INDICATOR restricts amplification to income-increasing accruals, so a cash-poor firm with conservative accruals receives exactly zero penalty and cannot enter the long leg on liquidity grounds alone. input_signals.hypothesis: Collection is directly observable as a shift in the composition of current assets: when cash rises as a share of current assets, receivables and inventory are being converted into money, and a cheap firm showing that shift is realizing the value its balance sheet claims rather than accumulating paper claims.

input_signals.reasoning: Rather than averaging two correlated horizons, this uses the firm's own three-year mean absolute accrual as the *scaling* denominator, converting the cross-sectional accrual level into a firm-specific standardized surprise — the only construction in the archive where the accrual is normalized by its own dispersion rather than by a balance-sheet or income deflator. The denominator is an absolute value so it cannot invert the sign, and the mechanism is economically distinct from the earlier difference-from-mean surprise because it identifies unusual accrual *magnitude relative to habitual volatility*, which is what separates opportunistic reporting from ordinary business-model variation.

input_signals.hypothesis: The economically meaningful measure of accrual reliance is how much working-capital investment the firm absorbed per dollar of the operating profit it habitually earns; when a year's working-capital build-up rivals the firm's normal profit, the reported earnings have no cash counterpart.
input_signals.reasoning: The sign-inversion defect is repaired exactly where the critic located it: the deflator is now the three-year mean of absolute operating profit, which is strictly positive so loss-making firms can no longer be scored as clean, and the smoothing prevents a single near-zero EBITDA year from exploding the ratio. input_signals.name: ProfitDestinationCashVersusWorkingCapital

input_signals.hypothesis: Profit has to go somewhere, and where it goes reveals whether it was real: a cheap firm that sends earnings to shareholders as cash dividends has demonstrably converted profit into money, whereas one whose earnings disappear into growing receivables and inventory has not, so the net flow of profit toward owners versus toward working capital is the sharpest earnings-quality test available.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a new mechanism rather than another deflator: it places a hard cash outflow (dividends) and a soft accrual absorption on the same earnings-power scale and takes their difference, so it measures the *destination* of profit instead of only its accrual content. Because dividends and working-capital investment are largely independent decisions, the combined leg should carry information beyond the champion's accrual-only measure, and the dividend-gated test already showed the payout channel is informative (alpha 3.4%, t 3.20) without contaminating the gate.

input_signals.hypothesis: A business that must keep several years' worth of operating profit permanently locked in receivables and inventory has a structurally poor claim on its own book value, because that capital is illiquid and impairable; a cheap firm with a light working-capital stock relative to its earnings power owns assets it can actually monetize.

Because it needs no differencing, coverage should be at or above the champion's 0.110.

input_signals.name: DebtFundedWorkingCapitalAbsorption
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(ADD(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), RATIO(DELTA(dlc, 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)))), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The dangerous configuration is not accrual absorption alone but accrual absorption financed by short-term borrowing: when a cheap firm's profit disappears into receivables and inventory while its current debt simultaneously expands relative to earnings power, the working-capital cycle is being funded by lenders who can withdraw, which is the standard pre-distress sequence.
input_signals.reasoning: This asks a new economic question — the *funding source* of the accrual, measured as a flow of short-term credit — rather than reweighting tails of an existing leg to chase in-sample statistics, and it differs from the earlier cash-buffer and total-leverage tests, which used stock-based scarcity or debt-intensity multipliers rather than the contemporaneous change in current debt. Both components are placed on the same earnings-power scale so their sum is interpretable as "profit absorbed plus short-term credit drawn, per dollar of normal profit," and the leg stays continuous with no censoring or point mass.
